title: Sixteen years of filings
lede: Hollywood Entertainment filed annual reports for every year from 1996 to 2004, and Movie Gallery reported Hollywood Video as a segment for three more. After January 2008 Movie Gallery stopped filing, and the record is press reports.

blocks.title: Stores: built in six years, emptied in three
blocks.subtitle: Company-operated Hollywood Video stores at each date. Year ends to 2004; Movie Gallery’s fiscal year ends after that.
blocks.xLabel: Year end, then dates of later reports (not evenly spaced)

points.title: the IPO
points.text: 25 stores at the end of 1993, the year the company went public.[^1]

points.title: the binge
points.text: 1,615 stores at the end of 1999, and $533.9M of long-term obligations.[^2]

points.title: the pause
points.text: 1,801 stores at the end of 2001, after the company almost stopped building.[^3][^5]

points.title: the sale
points.text: 2,006 stores at the end of 2004. Movie Gallery signs nine days later.[^5]

points.title: the first bankruptcy
points.text: 1,646 stores in January 2008, with Movie Gallery in Chapter 11.[^13]

points.title: the second
points.text: 545 stores left after the February 2010 closures.[^17]

blocks.source: 1992–1996[^1]; 1997–1999[^2]; 2000–2004[^5]; January 1, 2006[^11]; December 31, 2006[^12]; January 6, 2008[^13]; February 2010, after announced closures[^17]. We found no count for the end of 2008 or 2009.

blocks.title: What Movie Gallery paid out to buy Hollywood
blocks.subtitle: Cash paid at the April 2005 acquisition, $ millions.
blocks.source: Movie Gallery, annual report for fiscal 2005.[^11] The total is derived: $862.1M + $384.7M. It was financed with about $180.0M of Hollywood’s cash, an $870.0M credit facility and $325.0M of 11% notes; the facility also replaced Movie Gallery’s own revolving credit line.[^11]
